abstract: Background: Substance use disorders (SUD) are associated with reward circuit disruptions and high rates of trauma. Trauma has been found to reduce propensity to engage frontal, limbic, and striatal regions during reward anticipation. However, the interactive effect of trauma and SUD on anticipatory reward circuitry remains unclear. Methods: To address this critical research gap, treatment-enrolled individuals with at least one SUD (N = 150; 78 female) completed questionnaires assessing childhood trauma and current posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and a monetary incentive delay (MID) task during functional magnetic resonance imaging. The MID task presented participants with cues predicting the delivery of no, small, and large monetary gains and avoidance of equally weighted losses. Linear mixed effects models examined the effect of trauma severity or PTSD on percent signal change for anticipation of monetary gains, extracted from a-priori striatal, prefrontal, and mesolimbic anatomic regions of interest. Results: 70.7% of individuals experienced significant childhood trauma and 63.3% met self-report symptom thresholds for probable PTSD. Current PTSD symptoms were positively associated with emotion dysregulation, emotional impulsivity, and drug craving, but were not related to anticipatory BOLD signal. Higher childhood trauma severity (but not current PTSD severity) was associated with lower anticipatory responses within the nucleus accumbens, caudate, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and anterior insula to both gain and loss cues. Conclusions: Childhood adversity is associated with blunted reward anticipation across striatal, prefrontal, and limbic circuitry. This highlights the importance of considering childhood trauma severity in SUD treatment, which may require targeted interventions beyond standard cognitive behavioral therapy to restore normative salience processing, such as striatal neuromodulation.
